articles.title: Dogmatic Bayesianism Disorder
articles.content:
Note: This humorously intended sarcastic blog post directly mimics classifications of psychological disorders in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of the American Psychological Association, but Dogmatic Bayesianism is not in the DSM-5 as an actual psychological disorder - for now.

 

Dogmatic Bayesianism Disorder

Diagnostic Criteria                                              F61.1

A. Individuals are convinced that they know what other people want to know.

 

B. Individuals believe that everyone who is not a Bayesian is wrong. They almost continuously try to convince others, and there is often a strong feeling others need to be ‘saved’.

 

C. Strong tendency to ridicule non-Bayesians, including historical figures. Karl Popper (who opposed Bayesianism, as it opens the door to dogmatism in science) is an especially common target.

 

D. A pervasive obsession with Bayesian statistics, and the use of p-values or hypothesis testing by others, at the expense of flexibility, openness, and acknowledging that other coherent statistical approaches exist to deal with uncertainty.

 

E. Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning. The forceful insertion of Bayesian statistics into conversations can drive away conversation partners, to the point where almost all social contact is restricted to other dogmatic Bayesians.

 

F. Individuals believe everyone else will become a Bayesian. Older dogmatic Bayesian often lose bets that everyone will have become a Bayesian by a specific year. If this bet is lost, they continue to claim everyone will become a Bayesian in the future and consider this a rationally updated belief.

 

Specify if:

Persistent: The disorder has been present for more than 12 months.

Specify current severity:

Dogmatic Bayesianism Disorder is specified as severe when an academic exhibits all symptoms of the disorder, at which point individuals are classified as having Bayesian Evangelical Syndrome (BES).

 

Prevalence

Less than 0.01% of the general population is affected, but prevalence is estimated to be at 1% to 2% in statistically inclined academics. Due to diagnostic criterion E prevalence can be up to 80% on certain internet forums. Men are more frequently affected than women, at a ratio estimated at 100:1 or greater.  

Development and course

Development of the condition often starts in the early thirties, but onset can occur at an older age, in which case the symptoms are often much more severe. There is currently no treatment, and dogmatic Bayesianism typically increases with age. In rare cases (less than 1%) spontaneous recovery seems to occur, after which individuals often experience prolonged feelings of shame and embarrassment.

Risk and Prognostic Factors

The disorder is more common in individuals with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

articles.title: On the reliability and reproducibility of qualitative research
articles.content:
With my collaborators, I am increasingly performing qualitative research. I find qualitative research projects a useful way to improve my understanding of behaviors that I want to explore with other methods in the future. For example, some years ago I performed qualitative interviews with researchers who believed their own research had no value whatsoever. Although I did not intend to publish these interviews, they provided important insights for other projects that I am engaged in now. I was involved in qualitative research on the assessment process of interdisciplinary research (Schölvinck et al., 2024), and we performed interviews to understand how researchers interpret a questionnaire we were developing that measures personal values in science (Kis et al., 2025). Together with Anna van ‘Veer I supervised Julia Weschenfelder who interviewed scientists on what they believed the value of their research was, and I have hired Julia as a PhD as part of a large project on the meaningful interpretation of effect sizes. She is planning interviews with researchers about what determined the maximum sample size they are willing to collect (if you want to be interviewed about this, reach out!). With Sajedeh Rasti, who is completing her PhD in my lab, we have spent the last 2 years interviewing people who played important roles in the creation of large-scale coordinated research projects in science.

As a supervisor, I am always very actively involved in research projects, and I joined as many of the (extremely interesting) interviews Sajedeh performed, and I listened to the audio recordings of all interviews that Julia performed to give my interpretation of what the scientists discussed when interviewed. Yet it never occurred to me to independently perform the thematic analysis for these interviews, and compare the themes we derived. I became aware of this peculiarity after reading a great qualitative paper analyzing open questions in a study on questionable research practices (Makel et al., 2025). In this paper, two teams independently analyze themes in the same set of open questions. They largely find the same themes, and conclude: “our two independent analysis teams reported themes that were generally similar or overlapping, suggesting a robustness of the findings. We believe this suggests that independent qualitative analyst teams with similar positionality can use unique analytic paths and reach largely similar destinations. This contributes to the ongoing conversation within the qualitative research community about whether reproducibility and replicability are relevant or possible in qualitative research”.


Sometimes you read a paper that makes perfect sense – of course two independent teams should reach the same conclusions when they qualitatively analyze the same data – and yet, it was not part of your workflow. This is especially peculiar, because we use this exact workflow when we code other data sources. For example, Sajedeh Rasti will soon share a preprint on papers written by large teams of scientists. In this paper, we classify these papers into different categories, depending on the interdependencies that require coordination (e.g., epistemic, logistical, financial, etc., see Rasti et al., 2025). Sajedeh and I double-coded papers, and we discussed our levels of agreement. This is the normal thing to do. It is strange that I never considered the same approach when the data comes from interviews.

 

Research on inter-rater reliability of thematic coding

I looked into the literature to search for papers similar to Makel et al., 2025, where the same qualitative data is analyzed by multiple coders to examine how reproducible the themes are that are identified in the data. There are many more papers than the few I will list here, and someone should write a paper summarizing this literature. But this is a Sunday morning blog post, and not a systematic review, so I will just present some papers that I found interesting.

Armstrong and colleagues had six researchers independently analyze the same single focus‑group transcript, and found “close agreement on the basic themes,” but substantial divergence in how those themes were interpreted and organized, with each analyst having “‘packaged’ the themes differently.” (Armstrong et al., 1997). The authors in this paper then go on and say these differences demonstrate the inherent subjectivity in qualitative research. But this is not the message I take away from this paper at all. All coders of any type of data will differ slightly in the details they highlight. What matters most in this project is not how in verbal summaries of the themes, researchers highlight different details – that is to be expected, but also largely irrelevant – but that there is such clear agreement on the themes identified. If I read the examples in the paper, the differences are mainly in detail, where some summarize the themes at a higher level, and others on a more detailed level. Those who summarize the themes at a detailed level will of course pick out specific details others did not mention – but this can easily be improved upon by instructing coders better about the level of detail at which results should be provided, and how details should be chosen in verbal summaries.

Campbell and colleagues (2013) provide a great example of the work needed to reach high inter-rater reliability. They say that “Reliability is just as important for qualitative research as it is for quantitative research” and argue that replicability problems stem less from disagreement over themes per se than from “the unitization problem—that is, identifying appropriate blocks of text for a particular code or codes,” which can “wreak havoc when researchers try to establish intercoder reliability for in-depth semistructured interviews.” Using their own empirical coding exercise, they show that even with a detailed codebook, intercoder reliability remained modest (“54 percent reliability on average”), reflecting the interpretive complexity of semistructured interviews where “more than one theme and therefore more than one code may be applicable at once.” However, when disagreements were resolved through discussion, intercoder agreement rose dramatically to 96%, and 91% of initial disagreements were resolved. In my view, qualitative research is nothing special in this respect, as it is often difficult to achieve high inter-rater reliability in any coding project. For example, we have the same difficulty in reaching agreement when we code what the main hypothesis in a scientific paper is in metascientific research projects (Mesquida et al., 2025).

The importance and challenges of clear coding instructions related to text-segmentation is also discussed in a classic paper on the reliability qualitative research (MacQueen et al., 1998). Based on extensive experience with qualitative research at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, MacQueen and colleagues offer useful suggestions on creating a codebook that will lead to high reliability. Through an iterative process in which multiple coders independently code the same text, compare results, and revise definitions, they show how disagreement over themes is an indication of ambiguous codes – and not an inherent limitation of qualitative research. Reproducibility can be achieved by repeatedly checking whether coders can “apply the codes in a consistent manner” and refining the codebook until agreement is acceptable. The authors argue that we should not expect that coders will naturally “see” the same themes, but that they can code the same themes reliably if researchers use a disciplined, transparent, and collective codebook development process that supports reproducible qualitative analysis without denying its interpretive character.

A realist ontology in qualitative research

The idea of reliability, or reproducibility (the two concepts become intertwined in a lovely way in qualitative research, as the coder is the measurement device, so to say) in qualitative research emerges most naturally from a scientific realist perspective on knowledge generation. There are qualitative researchers who adopt philosophical perspectives that attempt to argue reliability and reproducibility are not relevant for qualitative research. I have engaged with these ideas a lot over the years, and find them unconvincing. Seale and Silverman (1997) push back strongly against the idea that reliability would not apply in qualitative research, and write “We believe that such a position can amount to methodological anarchy and resist this on 2 grounds. First, it simply makes no sense to argue that all knowledge and feelings are of equal weight and value. Even in everyday life, we readily sort fact from fancy. Why, therefore, should science be any different? Second, methodological anarchy offers a clearly negative message to the audiences of qualitative health research, suggesting that its proponents have given up claims to validity.”

I am personally more sympathetic to the view expressed by Popay and colleagues (1998): “On one side, there are those who argue that there is nothing unique about qualitative research and that traditional definitions of reliability, validity, objectivity, and generalizability apply across both qualitative and quantitative approaches. On the other side, there are those postmodernists who contend that there can be no criteria for judging qualitative research outcomes (Fuchs, 1993). In this radical relativist position, all criteria are doubtful and none can be privileged. However, both of these positions are unsatisfactory. The second is nihilistic and precludes any distinction based on systematic or other criteria. If the first is adopted, then, at best, qualitative research will always be seen as inferior to quantitative research. At worst, there is a danger that poor-quality qualitative research, which meets criteria inappropriate for the assessment of such evidence, will be privileged.” There are unique aspects of reliability in qualitative research, but qualitative research will not be taken seriously by the majority of scientists if researchers do not engage with reliability at all.

O’Conner and Joffe provide a useful guide on how to achieve inter-coder reliability in qualitative research in psychology, based on their own extensive experience (O’Connor & Joffe, 2020). They argue that “ICR helps qualitative research achieve this communicative function by showing the basic analytic structure has meaning that extends beyond an individual researcher. The logic is that if separate individuals converge on the same interpretation of the data, it implies “that the patterns in the latent content must be fairly robust and that if the readers themselves were to code the same content, they too would make the same judgments” (Potter & Levine-Donnerstein, 1999, p. 266).” They highlight how there are both external incentives to care about reliability (as it can function as a signal of quality) but also has direct benefits for the researchers performing the qualitative research.

If you feel similarly, and want to educate your students about qualitative methods where reliability and reproducibility are important, there is a nice paper that can be used to introduce your students to realist ontologies in qualitative research by Lourie and McPhail (2024). They note how the methodology literature in qualitative research often engages with interpretivist-constructivist approaches. Among my own collaborators, this perspective is not seen as appealing, and we prefer to build our qualitative research from a realist ontology. In this philosophy, inter-rater reliability, and reproducibility, are important aspects in knowledge generation (Seale, 1999). A good textbook on applied thematic analysis from this perspective is Applied Thematic Analysis (Guest et al., 2012).

I am very grateful to Makel and colleagues for making me realize I had overlooked the importance of independent coding of themes in qualitative research, and establish inter-rater reliability or reproducibility in qualitative research.

 

Personal take-home messages

After reflecting on this topic, there are some points that I am taking away from the work on reliability or reproducibility of thematic coding.

First, independent thematic analysis, and comparing how we code qualitative data, should be a standard practice in the qualitative studies in my lab. The suggestions by MacQueen and colleagues provide useful guidance that we should follow. There is nothing special about qualitative data sources in this respect.

Second, we already ask all participants if we can share full transcripts, and many agree. In our case, as we primarily interview scientists, so we are in the lucky position that they value transparency and data sharing, and that the content of our interviews is not particularly sensitive. Data sharing is of course not always possible. For example, in my interviews on why researchers felt their own research lacked any value whatsoever, many did continue to receive funding for this research, and they would not want their actual thoughts about their research to become public. But where possible, we should share transcripts for independent re-analysis and re-use.

Third, we should use the same techniques to increase the reliability of our claims in qualitative research, as we do in quantitative research. I recently have been annoyed by some extremely biased qualitative studies in metascience, where the researchers who performed the research clearly wanted their work to lead to a very specific outcome. It is easy to tell the story you want in qualitative research, if you reject the idea of reliability. But in my lab, we use methods that prevent us from allowing us to say what we want to be true, if we are wrong. In my current research project, I reserved 8000 euro out of the 1.5 million euro budget to hire ‘red teams’ (Lakens, 2020) to criticize the studies before we perform them. However, I had planned to only use red teams for large quantitative studies. I now think that I should also use the red teams for the qualitative studies I planned in the proposal, to make sure the coding of themes is reliable.

 

References

Campbell, J. L., Quincy, C., Osserman, J., & Pedersen, O. K. (2013). Coding In-depth Semistructured Interviews: Problems of Unitization and Intercoder Reliability and Agreement. Sociological Methods & Research, 42(3), 294–320. https://doi.org/10.1177/0049124113500475

articles.title: New Papers: Optimal Filter Settings for ERP Research
articles.content:
Zhang, G., Garrett, D. R., & Luck, S. J. (in press). Optimal filters for ERP research I: A general approach for selecting filter settings. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14531 [preprint]

Zhang, G., Garrett, D. R., & Luck, S. J. (in press). Optimal filters for ERP research II: Recommended settings for seven common ERP components. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14530 [preprint]

What filter settings should you apply to your ERP data? If your filters are too weak to attenuate the noise in your data, your effects may not be statistically significant. If your filters are too strong, they may create artifactual peaks that lead you to draw bogus conclusions.

For years, I have been recommending a bandpass of 0.1–30 Hz for most cognitive and affective research in neurotypical young adults. In this kind of research, I have found that filtering from 0.1–30 Hz usually does a good job of minimizing noise while creating minimal waveform distortion.

However, this recommendation was based on a combination of informal observations from many experimental paradigms and a careful examination of a couple paradigms, so it was a bit hand-wavy. In addition, the optimal filter settings will depend on the waveshape of the ERP effects and the nature of the noise in a given study, so I couldn’t make any specific recommendations about other experimental paradigms and participant populations. Moreover, different filter settings may be optimal for different scoring methods (e.g., mean amplitude vs. peak amplitude vs. peak latency).

Guanghui Zhang, David Garrett, and I spent the last year focusing on this issue. First we developed a general method that can be used to determine the optimal filter settings for a given dataset and scoring method (see this paper). Then we applied this method to the ERP CORE data to determine the optimal filter settings for the N170, MMN, P3b, N400, N2pc, LRP, and ERN components in neurotypical young adults (see this paper and the table above).

If you are doing research with these components (or similar components) in neurotypical young adults, you can simply use the filter settings that we identified. If you are using a very different paradigm or testing a very different subject population, you can apply our method to your own data to find the optimal settings. We added some new tools to ERPLAB Toolbox to make this easier.

One thing that we discovered was that our old recommendation of 0.1–30 Hz does a good job of avoiding filter artifacts but is overly conservative for some components. For example, we can raise the low end to 0.5 Hz when measuring N2pc and MMN amplitudes, which gets rid of more noise without producing problematic waveform distortions. And we can go all the way up to 0.9 Hz for the N170 component. However, later/slower components like P3b and N400 require lower cutoffs (no higher than 0.2 Hz).

You might be wondering how we defined the “optimal” filter settings. At one level, the answer is simple: The optimal filter is the one that maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio without producing too much waveform distortion. The complexities arise in quantifying the signal-to-noise ratio, quantifying the waveform distortion, and deciding how much waveform distortion is “too much”. We believe we have found reasonably straightforward and practical solutions to these problems, which you can read about in the published papers.
articles.author: Steve Luck

articles.title: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.25109v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.
articles.author: Shwetanshu Singh, Mark Keavney, Mathieu Duteil, Meriem Mehri, Scott Blain

articles.title: When Should Deployed BCI Decoders Adapt? A Resource-Priced Ladder for Frozen EEG Trunks
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.25315v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When should a deployed MI decoder spend adaptation resources-not only how to adapt under shift? We study a thin control layer outside a frozen encoder: a resource ladder (factory -> Bayesian head -> affine map, with full fine-tune as an escape hatch) governed by regime-aware gating under a utility that prices accuracy, fit time, and label cost. The head is Bayesian in the conjugate sense: a Normal-Inverse-Wishart prior over the class conditional Gaussians in embedding space, updated in closed form (no gradients) as labelled trials arrive. Full estimators, constants, and the reanalysis code are in the companion paper and the ancillary bundle of this submission. Thesis: adaptation should be gated and capped, not always-on and not blindly fine-tuned. Evidence: (i) utility-max gating over-adapts on clean data that already carries session drift; a clean-referenced gate restores low false-entry rates (e.g. dropping the adaptation rate from 0.56 to 0.11 on field-like sessions, with the cascade staying on the factory decoder for ~87% of clean cells). (ii) Under severe synthetic stress, a lightweight LDA head matches or exceeds the frozen trunk's accuracy across five encoder architectures (n=155 subject x trunk cells, pooled across shared subjects), at ~23x lower fit time than full warm-start fine-tuning. Always-on baselines favor capping the default below full fine-tune. (iii) In two no-perturbation BNCI session checks the factory model transferred without intervention (no reliable head gain), so the control layer's value under natural drift is cost-efficiency and clean-safety rather than demonstrated accuracy gains. (iv) Adaptation severity does not follow a universal ordinal ladder across datasets, highlighting the need for dynamic gating over fixed adaptation policies.
articles.author: Sergey Musienko

articles.title: Modeling Learner-Technology Interaction Through Multilevel Gaze Transition Dynamics to Inform Usability in Online Learning
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.25294v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Gaze data provide fine-grained evidence of how learners engage with instructional content and interface elements, complementing conventional usability evaluation methods. However, eye-tracking analyses often examine within-slide visual attention and across-slide navigation separately, limiting understanding of learner interaction throughout extended learning experiences. This exploratory multi-method study integrated area-of-interest transitions, gaze entropy, slide-level navigation, and network-based representations to analyze seven eye-tracking recordings of high school students interacting with an AI-supported online biology lesson, complemented by three post-intervention focus groups. Results showed individual differences in within-slide gaze allocation and switching patterns. Learners followed shared navigation pathways but differed in revisiting and immediate return behaviors. The focus group findings highlighted positive perceptions of interactive materials and AI-generated feedback, alongside usability concerns related to navigation, interface clarity, and assessment guidance. Together, these outcomes show how integrating multilevel gaze analytics with learner perspectives can provide complementary evidence for identifying interaction trends relevant to usability evaluation. Future research should test this approach with larger, more diverse samples and examine relationships among gaze patterns, usability, and learning outcomes.
articles.author: Yueqi Weng, Jie "Jennifer" Lu, fan Yang

articles.title: AI-Induced Social Erosion: Using LLMs for Work Tasks Reduces Help-Seeking Intentions Towards Colleagues
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.25269v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative AI is becoming embedded in knowledge work as an intelligent collaborator to assist in completing tasks. However, this readily available assistance risks displacing key interactions through which colleague relationships are built and sustained at work. This paper leverages the concept of help-seeking behaviour to investigate whether and how AI usage shapes colleague relationships. We conducted an online experimental vignette study where 248 knowledge workers evaluated scenarios that systematically varied whether and how AI was used across different work tasks. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that AI-enabled work reduced help-seeking intentions compared to non-AI work across tasks, and especially for brainstorming. Visible AI usage was associated with greater help-seeking intentions towards colleagues, and individual contributors' colleague relationships were more vulnerable than managers. Our findings identify opportunities for workplace AI tools, practices, and policies to preserve colleague relationships in increasingly AI-integrated workplaces.
articles.author: Kevin Chow, Sophia Deng, Bowen He, Hanyi Min, Qiaosi Wang, Koustuv Saha, Vedant Das Swain

articles.title: AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.25263v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($\beta = -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($\beta = -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.
articles.author: Dora Zhao, Grace Wang, Yutong Zhang, Lujain Ibrahim, Robert E. Kraut, Diyi Yang

articles.title: Design and Evaluation of a Body-Machine Interface as an Alternative Control Paradigm for Pedal-based Sewing Machines
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.25261v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Body-machine interfaces (BoMIs) exploit body movements to control assistive devices; they have been evaluated primarily in tasks such as cursor control or robotic manipulation where the entire movement repertoire is devoted toward device control. However, tasks with multiple concurrent processes require the user to share the movement repertoire used for device control with other body movements for task execution. This issue is examined here in the context of sewing, where the sewing machine is typically controlled by a pedal in coordination with hand movements for guiding the fabric. We evaluated the learning of a trunk-controlled BoMI for sewing machine control, and compared it with conventional pedal control. Twenty-four novice participants (12 BoMI, 12 Pedal) completed 10 trials of a standardized sewing assessment followed by 3 trials of a transfer task. The BoMI mapped trunk movements to the sewing machine's full functional repertoire, which included continuous speed control of the needle, and discrete actions such as presser-foot and needle lifts. The two groups learned at comparable rates, showing similar completion times and error counts; for both groups, completion time reduced by approximately 30\%. Additional analyses showed that the BoMI group had fewer presser-foot lift errors during training and fewer errors on the first transfer trial. Both groups also exhibited similar subjective workload. These findings collectively demonstrate that a BoMI interface can support sewing-machine control during concurrent manual activity, highlighting the potential for using BoMIs for increasing accessibility in industrial workplace contexts.
articles.author: Ashrut Aryal, Rajiv Ranganathan, Ranjan Mukherjee

articles.title: Towards Restorative Urban Spaces: An Exploratory Field Study of Nature Videos on Public Multi-Display Signage
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.25259v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, multi-display signage (MDS) has become increasingly common in urban stations, plazas, and other public spaces, where it is primarily used to present advertisements and information. Beyond these conventional applications, MDS offers opportunities to shape people's experiences of public environments through spatially distributed and dynamic visual content. Motivated by the potential of mediated nature to support restorative experiences in urban environments, we conducted a nine-day exploratory field study in a free-admission area of a science museum, presenting artificial intelligence (AI)-generated nature videos across four displays and collecting 1,263 questionnaire responses. We combined three complementary analyses. First, structural equation modeling identified strong associations among perceived consistency across displays, presence, and self-reported restorative responses, consistent with our theoretically motivated model. Second, exploratory comparisons across video-presentation configurations revealed modest differences in consistency and restoration ratings, although these AI-generated videos did not significantly outperform the advertisement reference. Third, qualitative analysis of open-ended responses identified fascination, immersion, and restorative feelings, alongside concerns about naturalness, visual quality, and motion-related discomfort. Together, these findings provide empirical insights into MDS-mediated nature experiences, with implications for nature-video design and questionnaire refinement. They also inform a tentative conceptual extension of the model incorporating additional perceptual and evaluative factors.
articles.author: Yuri Mikawa, Takumi Yokosaka, Yuki Kubota, Kazushi Maruya

articles.title: Squoosh Bench: Evaluating UX-1 on 318 Historical Website A/B Tests
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.25200v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Experimentation teams must decide which proposed website changes to test with live traffic. We evaluated whether forecasts from simulated shoppers could inform that choice. We screened 412 historical website A/B tests and evaluated four systems on the 318 that ran longer than 21 days. Each system predicted an original win, a variant win, or an inconclusive result. Page roles were masked and recorded outcomes were withheld during inference. Squoosh UX-1, a model fine-tuned on human browsing data, simulated 1,000 shoppers per arm and correctly classified 267 of 318 outcomes (84.0%, 95% Wilson interval 79.5-87.6%, treating experiments as independent). Qwen3 Next 80B, the strongest general-purpose configuration on outcome accuracy, correctly classified 196 of 318 (61.6%). UX-1 favored the variant in 126 experiments. In the live tests, 118 of those variants won (93.7%), four lost, and four had inconclusive results. The remaining 192 experiments included 19 additional variant wins.
articles.author: Rohith Pasula, Johari Dramiga, Viraj Shah, Suzan Halim, Tyler Dooskin

articles.title: Open Response Explorer: a Structured Collaborative Writing System for Peer-Informed Open-Response Assignments
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.25169v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Peer-informed open-response assignments (where students view, connect, and learn from peer contributions) hold the potential to foster collaborative knowledge building, yet the unstructured nature of free-form prose prevents students from effectively comparing and making sense of peers' work. We present Open Response Explorer, an interface that recenters open responses on structured idea units through purpose-based writing and peer response exploration, augmented by common-role text segment highlighting for easy comparison. A within-subjects lab study (N=12) validated the usefulness and usability of the system, demonstrating how it shaped the open-response drafting and peer exploration practices. We discuss implications for purpose-centered authoring and exploration that transform free-form prose into structured, comparable, and collectively navigable knowledge artifacts.
articles.author: Ziwei Gu, Ruixuan Chen, Elena Glassman

articles.title: A Human-Centric Adaptive Multi-Fidelity Digital Twin Framework for Cyber-Physical Systems
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.25082v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Digital twins of cyber-physical systems must operate with scarce data, on assets that change after deployment, and for humans whose needs differ, yet existing implementations fix fidelity at design time and do not match the representation to the human or the task. This paper proposes a human-centric adaptive multi-fidelity digital twin framework that models the evolving human, the physical twin, and the digital twin core, and adds a human inference and adaptation function that estimates the human state, predicts the response, and adapts the representation. The framework defines low-, medium-, and high-fidelity tiers distinguished by adaptivity and by coupling, quantified as the ratio of the digital twin latency to the duration of the process step it follows. Three proof-of-concept instantiations are evaluated: a virtual reality tutor, a computer numerical control milling model, and an industrial training station. The low tier estimated learner sentiment with an accuracy of 0.86. The forecasters of the milling model and the training station, both medium-tier, showed a normalized error decline of 0.39 to 0.89 and a human adaptation gain of 1.16 to 1.51, but their latency exceeded the physical process step by 25 to 87 times. Only the station's vision model met the physical step. The tiers are separated by which functions adapt and where the latency constraint lies, not by a monotone increase in gain or coupling.
articles.author: Clarisa Grijalva-Lugo, Yu-Zheng Lin, Shalaka Satam, Sicong Shao, Jesus Pacheco, Soheil Salehi, Pratik Satam

articles.title: When Does Depth Matter For In-Context Learning? Adaptive Inference in Deep Transformers
articles.content:
arXiv:2606.16694v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Transformers perform computations through many successive attention and feedforward blocks, allowing them to learn complex correlations between a large collection of coupled variables. When does stacking successive attention-feedforward computations over many layers provide a computational advantage over a single transformer block? We address this question by examining in-context learning in generalized linear attention transformers. We first introduce a general theory of distributed inference in such transformers, subject to constraints on communication and depth. We show that such systems can exploit internal representations (`function vectors') to infer a latent context variable at increasingly finer scales over its layers. For an in-context linear regression task, the theory predicts that while one-layer transformers without feedforward blocks are optimal for Gaussian priors over the context variable, multi-layer transformers are superior for non-Gaussian, tree-like priors. Trained linear attention transformers reproduce quantitative predictions from the theory. Using causal key-patching experiments, we verify that function vectors in intermediate layers mediate adaptive routing of information. Our results suggest that depth and feedforward blocks enable transformers to implement adaptive inference, and this is advantageous when the distribution over latent variables has hierarchical structure.
articles.author: Ravin Raj, Gautam Reddy

articles.title: Modeling sequential cognitive states via population level cortical dynamics
articles.content:
arXiv:2605.02365v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: In this work, we propose a mathematical framework for cyclic and sequential patterns of brain activity, combining heteroclinic dynamics with discrete neural-field models. Under explicit structural and positivity assumptions on the prescribed activity patterns, we show that the resulting spatially discrete neural-field system supports neither heteroclinic cycles nor nonconstant periodic orbits. Heteroclinic dynamics, on the other hand, arise in Lotka--Volterra-type systems, but these equations do not directly correspond to neuronal processes. To bridge these descriptions, we use a $C^1$ version of the Universal Approximation Theorem to approximate a target vector field by a neural network interpretable as a high-dimensional Amari-type neural-field system. Each periodic solution of the reduced dynamics admits a unique periodic realization at the population level with the same minimal period. For three-dimensional heteroclinic targets, we establish sufficient conditions ensuring that the approximating vector field admits a unique hyperbolic attracting periodic orbit in a trapping channel surrounding the original heteroclinic cycle. As a proof of concept, we apply this construction to a Lotka--Volterra-type target phenomenologically representing sequential network activations associated with focused-attention meditation.
articles.author: M Virginia Bolelli (L2S), Luca Greco (L2S), Dario Prandi (CNRS, L2S)

articles.title: Hierarchical Latent Structure Learning through Online Inference
articles.content:
arXiv:2603.19139v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Learning systems must balance generalization across experiences with discrimination of task-relevant details. Effective learning therefore requires representations that support both. Online latent-cause models support incremental inference but assume flat partitions, whereas hierarchical Bayesian models capture multilevel structure but typically require offline inference. We introduce the \textbf{Hierarchical Online Learning of Multiscale Experience Structure (HOLMES) model}, a computational framework for hierarchical latent structure learning through online inference. HOLMES combines a variation on the nested Chinese Restaurant Process prior with sequential Monte Carlo inference to perform tractable trial-by-trial inference over hierarchical latent representations without explicit supervision over the latent structure. In simulations, HOLMES matched the predictive performance of flat models while learning more compact representations that supported one-shot backward transfer to higher-level latent categories. In a forward transfer task, HOLMES additionally achieved above-chance outcome prediction for stimuli with never-before-seen feature combinations, by exploiting abstract shape-level representations learned across diverse training instances. These results provide a tractable computational framework for discovering hierarchical structure in sequential data.
articles.author: Ines Aitsahalia, Kiyohito Iigaya

articles.title: Sensorimotor behavior from an untrained brain-and-nerve-cord connectome
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.33881v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Connectomes map the neurons and synapses of an adult fly's brain and nerve cord, but how much of behavior follows from the wiring is unknown. Here we turn one such connectome into a spiking network of 172,433 neurons with a published brain model's untuned parameters, and run it alone and inside a simulated body. Two fixed rules connect them: odors and looming objects set the firing of the sensory neurons, and the firing of the leg motor neurons moves the legs. Outside the body, a pathway of known function conducts when it supplies a few percent or more of its target's input. In the body, the fly navigates around obstacles to nearly every odor source. A rewiring that keeps each neuron's connection counts and signs reaches far fewer, and the fly's leg commands replayed with the senses off reach almost none. Navigation needs the measured wiring and sensory feedback. Dopamine-gated weakening of the mushroom body's output synapses turns approach to an odor into avoidance, and the learning is associative once one class of olfactory synapse is scaled. An untrained connectome supports a behavior and its learned reversal. The pathways it cannot drive show what the wiring diagram leaves out.
articles.author: John R. Minnick, Jesus Gonzalez-Ferrer, Jinghui Geng, Jason K. Eshraghian, Mohammed A. Mostajo-Radji, David Haussler, Mircea Teodorescu

articles.title: System-level nonequivalence between integrated information and expected free energy in noisy permutation networks
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.03735v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The free-energy principle (FEP) and active inference describe prediction and adaptation using generative models, whereas integrated information theory (IIT) examines intrinsic causal organization. Can knowledge of a network's prediction in its current state determine its intrinsic integration? We address this question using a fixed one-step state-risk expected free energy (EFE) and IIT system integrated information. Noisy binary permutation networks allow causal wiring to vary while local transition reliability remains fixed. From a homogeneous current state, different architectures have identical complete one-step predictive distributions, and thus identical EFE under common preferences and observation models. Nevertheless, multicycle architectures have zero whole-system IIT integration, while single cycles can be integrated. For an n-unit noisy single cycle with reliability {\eta}, we obtain the exact expression $\phi_s^{(n)}(\eta) = \min\{2\eta^n\log_2(2\eta), -n\log_2\eta\}$. We prove that the minimum-information partition cuts exactly two causal edges, establish a unique interior maximum, and show that, in the large-n limit, the optimal reliability approaches unity, the joint specified-state probability approaches one half, and the maximum system integrated information approaches one ibit. Independent computation corroborates these results. Local surprisal-coordinate identities can be expressed through optimized variational free energy under exact inference, but this algebraic identity does not establish that a neural system performs variational inference. The counterexample establishes a state-conditioned non-identifiability limit for the specified EFE, not an incompatibility between IIT and the FEP. Bridging the two descriptions requires intervention-sensitive information beyond this single predictive distribution.
articles.author: Katsuaki Tanabe

articles.title: Accurate EEG-based linear state-space model of cortical dynamics during a passive motor task with exogenous input
articles.content:
arXiv:2510.02596v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Revealing the dynamics of the brain in the presence of exogenous inputs is crucial for mechanistic understanding, interventions and regulations. We study state-space mathematical modeling of brain's cortical dynamics using electroencephalography (EEG) data in an experiment with continuous exogenous input. We use subspace identification techniques to model the brain dynamics in a passive motor task experiment. The EEG data were recorded while participants were seated with their wrist strapped to a haptic manipulator. The manipulator imposed a continuous multisine angular perturbation to the wrist as the exogenous input to the brain. Using two subspace identification algorithms, we show that linear time-invariant state-space models accurately represent the measurements, in a latent space, assuming that the EEG data are the models' output. The model is verified and validated using data from seven participants. Moreover, we construct linear maps to relate the latent space dynamics to the neural source space. We verify that the findings of our model align with those identified in previous studies. Accurate linear model in the presence of exogenous input provides a pathway for designing parsimonious and simple controllers. In addition, it enables development of online monitoring, connectivity analysis and control relevant to neurorehabilitation, motor learning, and brain-computer interfacing.
articles.author: Sanna Bakels, Mark van de Ruit, Matin Jafarian
